name: Rolling 12/8 down-up
rationale: A gentle 12/8 roll: a down strum on every beat with a light upstroke on the last triplet of the beat. The quiet version only rings two long chords per bar with an up flick before beat 4, and its bar 4 holds one chord for the whole bar. The busy version strums every beat and in bar 4 lets beat 3 ring and pushes a ringing upstroke into the next bar.

name: Bass note, then soft triplet strums
rationale: The thumb picks the bass note on beats 1 and 3, and soft strums fill the following triplets, a slow 12/8 boom-strum. The quiet version strums only once after each bass note; the busy version fills nearly every triplet with down-up strums. Bar 4 drops the second bass note and lets a long chord ring from beat 3.

name: Long ringing chord, light upstroke answer
rationale: Each bar opens with a chord left to ring for most of the bar, answered by a soft ringing upstroke on the last triplet, so the guitar breathes with the vocal. The busy version splits the bar into two ringing halves, each followed by a quick down-up. Bar 4 of the quiet version is one whole-bar chord with a fret slide; the busy bar 4 stops on beat 3 and leaves a held chord.

name: Slow shuffle swing
rationale: A slow shuffle: long downs on beats 1 and 3 and a swung down-up on beats 2 and 4, so the backbeat has a lilting triplet bounce. The busy version keeps the bounce on every beat and adds an extra down on the middle triplet of beat 4. Bar 4 of both versions finishes with a ringing chord pushed onto the last triplet of beat 4.

name: Six-eight sway
rationale: Felt in two big swings per bar: a long chord on beats 1 and 3 and a single soft strum on the middle triplet of beats 2 and 4. The busy version rocks through each half with a strum on the third triplet and a down-up in the second beat. Bar 4 of the quiet version rings the whole bar out; the busy bar 4 ends with a rising triplet of downs into the next bar.

name: Chord with triplet arpeggio answer
rationale: Two ringing chords per bar, each followed by two picked upper strings (plus a light upstroke before beat 3) on the triplets of the next beat, like a pianist answering the chord. The busy version strums every beat with an up flick after beats 2 and 4, keeping one picked note. Bar 4 of the quiet version picks a falling three-note line before the next bar; the busy bar 4 rings a chord for the last two beats.

name: Soul ballad backbeat triplets
rationale: A soul-ballad comp: the guitar leaves beats 1 and 3 to the bass and plays a soft down-up-down triplet on beats 2 and 4. The busy version adds short downs on beats 1 and 3 and an up on the last triplet of beat 3, so the triplet pulse never stops. Bar 4 of both versions ends with a long chord on beat 4 that rings into the next bar, with a muted scratch before it.

name: Gospel triplet push
rationale: A churchy soul-ballad feel: a long chord carries most of the bar and a pickup upstroke on the last triplet of beat 3 leads into a ringing beat 4. The busy version strums a down on beats 2 and 3 with triplet pickups, landing on a long beat 4. Bar 4 pushes the next chord early, on the last triplet of beat 4, left ringing over the bar line.

name: Brushed alternating triplets
rationale: A soft brush of the strings on every triplet, the hand moving down and up continuously, like brushes on a snare. The quiet version only brushes beats 1 and 3, leaving beats 2 and 4 silent; the busy version keeps the brush going through all twelve triplets. Bar 4 settles onto a long chord on beat 3 in both versions.

name: Power-ballad verse swell
rationale: For a power ballad that starts quiet: the verse rings a long down on beat 1 and a long upstroke on beat 3, almost a pad, then fills bar 4 with a rising triplet strum into the next phrase. The chorus version strums long chords on beats 1 and 3 with two downs on the last triplets of beats 2 and 4, a building 12/8 drive. Its bar 4 ends with a triplet run of downs.

name: Picked bass with triplet up-flicks
rationale: The thumb picks a bass note on every beat, alternating the root and the next string, while the hand flicks a light upstroke on the last triplet of beats 2 and 4. The busy version strums around every bass note with a down on the middle triplet and an up on the last one. Bar 4 stops the bass on beat 3 and rings a chord.

name: Half-time 12/8 build
rationale: A slow build for a ballad that is gathering strength: the verse holds a chord through almost three beats and then answers with a down-up on the last triplets. The chorus version moves to full triplet strumming on beats 2 and 4 around long chords on 1 and 3. Bar 4 of the verse rings a whole-bar chord; bar 4 of the chorus stops on beat 3 and lets it ring.

name: Triplet pickup into the one
rationale: Every bar ends with a quick down-up on the last two triplets that rolls into the next downbeat, the ballad equivalent of a drum pickup. The quiet version is otherwise just two long chords; the busy version strums the whole bar in a down-down-up triplet bounce. Bar 4 ends both versions with a pushed ringing chord on the last triplet.

name: Nylon rocking bass and strum
rationale: A nylon-string figure: a picked bass note on every beat, rocking between the root and an inner string, with a soft strum on the last triplet of each beat. The busy version strums the last two triplets of every beat, down then up. Bar 4 slows to a single long chord on beat 3 after two beats of the figure.

name: Ringing upstroke swells
rationale: A long chord on beat 1 is answered by a ringing upstroke on the last triplet of beat 2, which swells through the second half of the bar. The busy version keeps the upstroke swell and adds a down on beat 2 and a down-up-down triplet on beat 4. Bar 4 rings a single long chord in the quiet version and ends the busy one on a ringing beat 3.

name: Hymn chord with rising arpeggio
rationale: A hymn-like pattern: one chord rings for three beats while the fingers pick a rising three-note triplet arpeggio on beat 4 that leads into the next chord. The busy version strums on every beat with a triplet down-up-down on beat 4 under the same arpeggio idea. Bar 4 of the quiet version drops the arpeggio and answers the chord with a ringing upstroke on the last triplet of beat 3; the busy bar 4 rings beats 3 and 4.

name: Down-down-up triplet bounce
rationale: A rolling bounce where each beat is down, down, up on the triplets, giving a warm continuous swing for a full chorus. The quiet version alternates a down-up beat with a long ringing beat. Bar 4 of the quiet version holds a chord from beat 2; bar 4 of the busy version breaks off with a ringing chord on beat 3 and a pickup upstroke.

name: Anticipated second chord
rationale: The second chord of each bar arrives early, on the last triplet of beat 2, and rings through the rest of the bar, which gives a sighing, leaning feel. The busy version anticipates every beat 3 and beat 4 the same way with short strums in between. Bar 4 of both versions pushes the next downbeat onto the last triplet of beat 4.

name: Power-ballad 12/8 chorus
rationale: A big 12/8 power-ballad chorus: a ringing down on every beat with an upstroke on the last triplet, and an extra down on beat 4 to drive into the next bar. The verse version is two long chords with a down-up on beat 3. Bar 4 of the chorus lands on a chord held from beat 3 with a fret slide into the next section.

name: Fifties triplet chops
rationale: The old soul-ballad triplet comp: short down chops on every triplet, very light, like the piano in a fifties slow dance. The quiet version only chops the triplets of beats 2 and 4; the busy one chops all twelve. Bar 4 stops the chops on beat 3 and lets a chord ring out.

name: Ringing chord with bass walk
rationale: A chord rings for three beats and the thumb walks up three bass strings on the triplets of beat 4 into the next chord. The busy version strums on beats 1, 2 and 3 with light ups, keeping the bass walk on beat 4. Bar 4 of the quiet version replaces the walk with a short down-up strum figure.

name: Swaying down and up
rationale: A swaying motion felt in two halves per bar: a long down on beats 1 and 3 and a single upstroke on the middle triplet of beats 2 and 4. The busy version adds a down-up on the second and third triplets of each half. Bar 4 ends both versions with a soft muted scratch and a ringing chord on beat 4.

name: Held chord, then triplet lift
rationale: The verse holds a chord nearly the whole bar and lets a ringing upstroke on the last triplet of beat 3 carry it over, leaving room for a rubato-sounding vocal. The chorus rings beats 1 and 2 and then lifts with continuous down-up-down triplets on beats 3 and 4. Bar 4 of the verse fills beat 4 with a triplet run; bar 4 of the chorus rings a whole-bar chord.

name: Triplet strum with a breath on 3
rationale: The first half of the bar moves in triplet strums and then the hand stops on a long chord on beat 3, a breath in the middle of the phrase. The busy version strums full triplets on beats 1 and 2 and adds a down-up on beat 4. Bar 4 of both versions rests through beat 4 after the long chord.

name: Picked triplets with backbeat stabs
rationale: A soul-ballad texture: the fingers pick the bass and two upper strings as a triplet on beats 1 and 3, and a short strum stab marks beats 2 and 4. The busy version adds upstrokes on the last triplets and a down-up-down on beat 4. Bar 4 ends on a long chord on beat 4 with a fret squeak before it.

name: Quarter-note triplet climax
rationale: Strums on quarter-note triplets (three even strums across two beats), the two-against-three lift that ballads use for a climax. The quiet version plays the quarter-note triplet in the first half and then rings a chord, and its bar 4 plays the triplet through the whole bar as a build. The busy version fills between the quarter-note triplets with light upstrokes, and its bar 4 is one long chord.

name: Slow even eighths
rationale: Straight slow eighths for a pop ballad: long downs on beats 1 and 3, each answered by an up on the next "and". The busy version strums down-up eighths through the whole bar with a ringing chord on beat 1. Bar 4 of the quiet version rings the whole bar; the busy bar 4 pushes the next chord on the "and" of 4.

name: Sixteenth lilt
rationale: A gentle sixteenth-note lilt: long chords on 1 and 3 with a soft down on the "and" of 1 and an up on the last sixteenth of the bar. The busy version adds sixteenth upstrokes after each "and", so the bar dances lightly. Bar 4 of both versions pushes the next chord onto the last sixteenth, left ringing.

name: Bass and strum, straight
rationale: A straight boom-strum: the thumb plays the bass on beats 1 and 3 and a strum answers on beats 2 and 4. The busy version adds upstrokes on the "and" of every beat around the strums. Bar 4 picks only the first bass note and rings a chord from beat 3.

name: Long chord, sixteenth flick
rationale: One chord rings for most of the bar, with a single light up flick on the last sixteenth leading into the next chord. The busy version strums the first half long, then fills the second half with sixteenth downs and ups. Bar 4 of the quiet version adds a fret slide before the next bar; the busy bar 4 ends on a long chord from beat 3.

name: Pushed and-of-two
rationale: The second chord of the bar is pushed onto the "and" of beat 2 and left ringing, a classic slow-ballad syncopation. The busy version strums eighths around the same pushed long chord. Bar 4 of the quiet version also pushes the next bar onto the "and" of 4; the busy bar 4 stops on the pushed chord.

name: Quarter-note pulse
rationale: A plain, steady quarter-note strum for a sparse piano-led ballad, with the first chord of each bar left to ring longer. The busy version adds upstrokes on the "and" of beats 1, 3 and 4. Bar 4 of the quiet version holds a chord from beat 2; the busy one pushes on the "and" of 4.

name: Half notes with sixteenth pickup
rationale: Two ringing half-note chords per bar with a soft sixteenth upstroke pickup just before the next bar. The busy version plays a dotted down-up on each beat, swinging gently on the last sixteenth. Bar 4 of the quiet version holds one chord; bar 4 of the busy version ends with a ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Soft three-three-two
rationale: Three ringing chords per bar grouped three, three and two eighths (beats 1, the "and" of 2, and 4), a soft syncopation that keeps a ballad from feeling square. The busy version fills the gaps with upstrokes and a down on beat 3. Bar 4 of both versions rings out from the "and" of 2.

name: Acoustic sixteenth chorus
rationale: A fuller acoustic chorus in sixteenths: down on each beat, a down on the "and" of 1 and 3, and quick ups on the last sixteenths. The quiet version keeps only the down-up on beats 1 and 3 with long chords on 2 and 4. Bar 4 of the busy version stops on a ringing beat 3, with a muted scratch before it.

name: Ringing one, chopped backbeat
rationale: A long chord on beat 1 and short, damped chops on beats 2 and 4, so the guitar marks the backbeat without crowding the vocal. The busy version adds upstrokes on the "and" of 2 and 3 and a sixteenth pickup at the end. Bar 4 of both versions holds a long chord from beat 3.

name: Soul ballad sixteenth flicks
rationale: Long chords on beats 1 and 3 with light upstroke flicks on the off-sixteenths, the soul-ballad way of keeping a slow tempo moving. The quiet version flicks only once per half bar. Bar 4 of both versions pushes the next chord onto the last sixteenth.

name: Dotted-eighth echo
rationale: Strums spaced a dotted eighth apart (beat 1, the last sixteenth of 1, the "and" of 2) give an echo-like, floating rhythm over a slow ballad. The quiet version rings a half-note chord and then two soft upstrokes on the dotted spacing. Bar 4 of both versions rings a long chord from beat 3.

name: Power-ballad eighth-note drive
rationale: For the big chorus of a power ballad: steady down strums on every eighth, with an up only on the last "and", driving and full. The verse version is a long chord with a soft down-up on the "and" of 3 and on 4. Bar 4 of the chorus ends with a long chord on the "and" of 4, pushed into the next bar.

name: Stop and lift
rationale: The quiet version rings a chord, rests, and then plays a short down and an up at the end of the bar, so each bar breathes before lifting into the next. The busy version strums through the bar and finishes with a run of sixteenths on beat 4. Bar 4 of both versions is a stop: one long chord from beat 1 that rings through the bar.
